planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Mariesii, discovered in Japan in 1879, is the classic lacecap hydrangea from which many later lacecap cultivars descend.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Discovered in Japan in 1879 by plant collector Charles Maries, this hydrangea is the classic lacecap form, with a flat outer ring of large, showy sterile florets surrounding a central disk of small, fertile true flowers, a more delicate and naturalistic look than the familiar rounded mophead. Like other Hydrangea macrophylla cultivars its color shifts with soil pH, opening blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil; amend with aluminum sulfate to intensify blue tones in the alkaline soils common across the Gulf South. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering to shape, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent wilting.

common_name: Madame Emile Mouilliere Hydrangea (Antique White Mophead with Colored Eye)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this French cultivar dates to 1909 and remains one of the finest white mopheads.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Introduced in France in 1909, Madame Emile Mouillere bears large, rounded, pure white mophead blooms with a delicate pink or blue eye at the center of each floret depending on soil pH, a refined color combination that has kept it in cultivation for well over a century. Unlike the fully pH-responsive blue-or-pink cultivars, its white petals stay white regardless of soil chemistry, while only the small central eye shifts color, giving a subtler, more restrained effect than a fully colored mophead. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in the Gulf South to prevent wilting in peak summer heat.

common_name: Generale Vicomtesse de Vibraye Hydrangea (Antique French Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this old French cultivar shifts reliably between clear pink and true blue depending on soil pH.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. One of the older named French mophead hydrangeas still grown, Generale Vicomtesse de Vibraye is prized for producing an especially clean, true color shift, opening a clear rose-pink in alkaline soil and a rich, saturated blue in acidic soil, making it a favorite for gardeners wanting to demonstrate or fine-tune the classic hydrangea pH effect. The rounded flower heads are medium-sized and produced in good quantity on a compact, well-branched shrub. It blooms on old wood, so limit pruning to right after flowering, and provide morning sun with afternoon shade in hot Southern climates to keep the blooms from wilting.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Otaksa is among the oldest named hydrangea cultivars, introduced to the West from Japan in the 19th century.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Otaksa is one of the earliest named hydrangea cultivars introduced to Western gardens from Japan in the 19th century by the plant collector Philipp von Siebold, who reportedly named it after a Japanese companion. Its large, rounded mophead blooms shift between rose-pink and blue depending on soil pH, in the same manner as later cultivars, and its historic significance lies in being one of the founding introductions behind the whole class of garden mophead hydrangeas grown today. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and site it with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent wilting.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Ayesha is instantly recognizable for its unusual cupped, hooded petals that resemble a lilac cluster rather than a typical hydrangea floret.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Ayesha is one of the most distinctive hydrangea cultivars in cultivation, its individual florets cupped and curled inward so tightly that a full flower head looks remarkably like a cluster of lilac blooms rather than the flat-petaled florets typical of the species, in shades of lilac-mauve to soft blue depending on soil pH. Beyond its unusual form, some gardeners report a faint sweet fragrance from the blooms, a rare trait in mophead hydrangeas. It blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates to keep blooms from wilting.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Altona is a vigorous older German cultivar known for exceptionally sturdy flower stems.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Altona bears large, rounded mophead blooms in carmine-rose in alkaline soil, shifting to true blue in acidic soil, on notably sturdy stems that hold the heavy flower heads upright through wind and rain better than many older mophead cultivars. Its vigorous, reliable growth and dependable, long-lasting blooms have kept it in commerce since its introduction in Germany decades ago. It blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering, and give it morning sun with afternoon shade in hot Southern climates to prevent wilting.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on an extremely sturdy pergola or arbor built to carry the mature vine's substantial weight.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on an extremely sturdy support structure, since mature vines become massive and heavy over time. Macrobotrys is grown above all for its astonishing flower racemes, violet-blue and fragrant, that can trail two to three feet long, among the longest of any wisteria, creating a dramatic curtain effect when trained over a tall pergola where the full length of each raceme can hang free. Like other Japanese wisteria it twines clockwise and is a vigorous, potentially aggressive grower that needs firm annual pruning, both in summer to control rampant new growth and in late winter to shape and encourage flower bud formation. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity, and be prepared for a genuinely large, long-term structural commitment in the landscape.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Alba is a white-flowered form of Japanese wisteria grown for its long, fragrant racemes.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a very sturdy support structure built to carry the mature vine's considerable weight. Alba bears long, pendulous racemes of pure white, intensely fragrant flowers in spring, offering a softer, more luminous alternative to the classic violet-blue wisteria for a moon garden, evening seating area, or pairing with darker-flowered companions. Like other Japanese wisteria it twines clockwise and grows vigorously, requiring firm summer pruning of rampant new growth and a shaping late-winter prune to encourage flower buds rather than rampant vegetative growth. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity and plan for a genuinely large, long-term structure to support it.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Rosea is a soft pink-flowered form of Japanese wisteria, an unusual color among wisterias.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a very sturdy support structure built to carry the mature vine's considerable weight. Rosea bears long, fragrant racemes in an unusual pale, dusty pink, a soft, romantic departure from the violet-blue or white that dominates most wisteria, making it a distinctive choice for a pastel garden scheme. Like other Japanese wisteria it twines clockwise and grows vigorously, needing firm summer pruning to control rampant new growth and a shaping late-winter prune to encourage flowering rather than pure vegetative sprawl. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity and plan for a genuinely large, long-term structure to support it.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Prolific is a heavy-flowering Chinese wisteria selection valued for consistent, abundant bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a very sturdy support structure built to carry the mature vine's considerable weight. Prolific was selected from Chinese wisteria specifically for its reliably heavy flowering, opening dense, fragrant, violet-blue racemes all at once before the leaves fully emerge, in the classic Chinese wisteria style, for a bolder, more uniform floral display than seedling-grown plants often produce. Like other Chinese wisteria it twines counterclockwise, in contrast to the clockwise twining of Japanese wisteria, and is a vigorous, potentially aggressive grower that needs firm annual pruning both in summer and late winter to control growth and encourage flowering. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity and plan for a genuinely large, long-term structural commitment.

common_name: Alba Chinese Wisteria (Fragrant White-Flowered Chinese Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; this white-flowered form of Chinese wisteria opens its blooms all at once for a dramatic display.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a very sturdy support structure built to carry the mature vine's considerable weight. This white-flowered form of Chinese wisteria bears dense, fragrant racemes that open nearly simultaneously along the vine before the leaves fully emerge, in the classic Chinese wisteria style, creating a striking curtain of white bloom rather than the more staggered, trailing display typical of Japanese wisteria. It twines counterclockwise, opposite the direction of Japanese wisteria, and grows vigorously, requiring firm pruning both in summer to control rampant growth and in late winter to shape and encourage flower bud formation. Give it several years to reach flowering maturity and plan for a genuinely large, long-term structure to support it.

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy pergola or arbor; Wisteria brachybotrys is a less commonly grown Japanese species valued for large individual flowers on shorter racemes.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support structure. Shiro-kapitan belongs to the less commonly grown silky wisteria species, distinguished by soft, velvety foliage and shorter but denser racemes of unusually large, pure white, intensely fragrant flowers compared to the longer, more open racemes of Japanese wisteria. Its more compact raceme length and refined flower size make it a good choice for gardeners who want the wisteria experience on a slightly smaller scale than the sprawling Macrobotrys-type cultivars. Like other wisteria it needs firm annual pruning, both in summer to control vigorous new growth and in late winter to shape and encourage flowering, and several years to reach flowering maturity on a genuinely sturdy long-term support.
